After every presentation I ask at least two questions, and I want to explain why, because a lot of people take it personally. The first question is almost always about the source of a number. Where did this come from? How was it calculated? I am not attacking the speaker. I am checking whether the speaker knows the business behind the slide. The second question is usually a hypothetical. What would happen if the market changed, or if your biggest client left? I do not expect a perfect answer. I want to see how the person thinks. The worst answer is a long one that avoids the question. The best answer is short: it repeats my question in one sentence, gives a direct answer, and stops. And if the speaker does not know, I would much rather hear that he will get back to me than a number that somebody invented on the spot.

The first time I took questions in English, I was not worried about the presentation. I was worried about the questions, because I could not prepare them. And the first one came very fast, with an accent I did not know. I understood maybe half of it. So I did something I had never done in Portuguese. I said, sorry, could you repeat the last part of the question? She repeated it, more slowly, and it was easy. Nobody in the room cared. The second thing I learned was to make my questions indirect when I needed something from a director. Instead of saying, when will you decide, I said, could you tell me when you expect to decide? It was the same question, but it sounded like a partner, not a supplier. And the third thing: write down every question you could not answer, and answer it by email the next day. That email did more for my reputation than the whole presentation.

So your question is whether the growth will continue next year. The short answer is yes. Off the top of my head, the ballpark figure is two more percentage points. I will check the exact number and get back to you by Friday.
